```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs
from funs import DSText

import spacy

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"
```

```{python}
#| tags: [remove]
#| include: false
ub = ""
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
docs = (
    pl.read_parquet(ub + "data/agnews_pca.parquet")
    .filter(c.index == "test")
    .select(c.id, c.label, c.text)
    .rename({"id": "doc_id"})
    .sort(c.doc_id)
    .group_by(c.label, maintain_order=True)
    .head(50)
)
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
anno = DSText.process(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.text), nlp)
```

### Questions

`docs` and `anno` hold 200 short AG News articles, 50 each labeled `"Business"`,
`"Sci/Tech"`, `"Sports"`, and `"World"`. Each row of `docs` has a `doc_id`, the
topic `label`, and the `text` of the article.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save
it to a variable.

1. Using `docs`, count the number of articles with each `label`.

```{python}
(
    docs
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
)
```

2. Filter `anno` to the alphabetic tokens with `.filter(c.is_alpha)`, count the
number of times each `lemma` appears, sort from most to least common, and keep the
first 15 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

Almost all of these are short, common words. The exceptions are `say`, which wire
stories use to quote people, and `AP` and `Reuters`, the news services that sent the
articles. None of them tells us the topic of an article.

3. Take the code from the previous question and draw it as a bar plot with
`geom_col`, with `lemma` on the x-axis and the count on the y-axis. Add
`coord_flip()` so the labels are readable.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(15)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lemma, c.n))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

4. Find the document frequency of each lemma: the number of articles it appears in.
Filter to the alphabetic tokens, group by `lemma`, and use
`n_docs = c.doc_id.n_unique()` inside of `.agg`. Sort from most to fewest documents
and keep the first 15 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n_docs = c.doc_id.n_unique())
    .sort(c.n_docs, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

"the" appears in 163 of the 200 articles. A word that appears in most of the
articles cannot tell them apart, and TF-IDF gives these words a low weight.

5. Compute the TF-IDF scores with
`DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)` and print the result.

```{python}
DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
```

Each row is one lemma in one article. `df_docs` is the document frequency from
question 4, and `tfidf` is large when a lemma is common in the article but rare in
the corpus. Setting `max_df=0.5` removes every lemma that appears in more than 100
articles, so "the", "to", "a", "in", and "of" are gone.

6. Take the code from the previous question and find the 10 terms with the highest
TF-IDF score in each article, joined together into a single string, as in the
chapter.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
```

7. Take the code from the previous question and join it to
`docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label)`. Then sort by `label` and `doc_id` and keep the
first two articles of each label with `.group_by(c.label, maintain_order=True).head(2)`.
Before looking at the `label` column, try to guess each article's topic from its
terms.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .sort(c.label, c.doc_id)
    .group_by(c.label, maintain_order=True)
    .head(2)
)
```

Some are easy to guess: `doc120027` (Phelps, medley, Gold) is Sports and
`doc120033` (chief, Canadian, police) is World. Others are harder, and words like
"he", "his", and "for" still show up because each one appears in fewer than half of
the articles.

8. A "document" does not have to be a single article. Join `anno` to
`docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label)` and pass the result to `DSText.compute_tfidf` with
`max_df=0.75` and `doc_name="label"`. This treats all 50 articles with the same
label as one document. Find the 10 terms with the highest score for each label, as
in question 6 but with `label` in place of `doc_id`.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(
        anno.join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id),
        max_df=0.75,
        doc_name="label"
    )
    .sort([c.label, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.label)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
```

Pooling the articles gives a clearer picture of each topic, such as "profit",
"oil", and "price" for Business and "olympic" and "medal" for Sports. Pronouns like
"he" and "his" still appear, because with only four documents, `max_df=0.75` removes
a word only if it appears in all four.

9. Take the code from the previous question, but leave off the last `.group_by` and
`.agg`. Draw a bar plot with `geom_col`, with `lemma` on the x-axis and `tfidf` on
the y-axis. Add `coord_flip()` and `.facet_wrap("label", scales="free")`.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(
        anno.join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id),
        max_df=0.75,
        doc_name="label"
    )
    .sort([c.label, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.label)
    .head(10)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lemma, c.tfidf))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
    .facet_wrap("label", scales="free")
)
```
